what: Sezzle lets shoppers pay in instalments. At checkout, a customer splits a purchase into four payments over six weeks instead of paying at once; Sezzle pays the merchant immediately and collects from the shopper. It also sells a subscription giving shoppers more flexible terms.
customers: Online and in-store shoppers, mostly younger and with limited credit history, and the merchants who offer Sezzle at checkout to increase conversion.
money: Fees from merchants and late or rescheduling fees from consumers.
Monthly fees for Sezzle Premium and Anywhere, which give shoppers more flexibility.
moat: The subscription product is the distinctive piece: instead of depending only on merchant fees, Sezzle charges consumers a monthly fee for access, which is recurring revenue that does not require a purchase to occur. Underwriting each instalment plan individually, with short durations, also lets the company adjust credit risk quickly as data arrives.
risks: This is consumer lending to shoppers with limited credit history, and credit losses are the risk that has periodically destroyed this entire category.
The shares trade at about 28.1 times earnings, 8.5 times sales and 20.2 times EV/EBITDA, a high price for a lender.
Revenue has grown extraordinarily fast — $159.4M in 2023 to $450.3M in 2025 — and such growth in lending usually precedes a credit reckoning.
Regulation of buy-now-pay-later lending is tightening in several countries, and rules on affordability checks and reporting would raise costs.
Only six analysts cover the stock, so the $192.67 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Last year’s net margin was 29.6%, and free cash flow was $297.6M on $581.6M of revenue.
The subscription revenue is recurring and does not require a purchase to occur, which is unusual in this category.
Instalment plans last six weeks, so credit problems surface quickly and the book can be adjusted fast.
Revenue has grown from $114.8M in 2021 to $581.6M trailing, which is exceptional growth.
Debt of $140.8M against $64.1M of cash is modest relative to the cash generation.
watch: Loss rates on the instalment book, and subscription revenue growth. Growth in lending is easy and credit is the only thing that determines whether it was worth having.
view: Buy-now-pay-later is consumer lending with better marketing, and that framing should come first. Sezzle pays the merchant immediately and collects four payments from the shopper over six weeks. If the shopper pays, Sezzle earns a merchant fee and possibly a late fee. If enough shoppers do not pay, the economics invert. Everything else about this business is secondary to the loss rate.

The growth has been extraordinary — revenue from $159 million in 2023 to $582 million trailing — and extraordinary growth in a lending business is precisely the pattern that precedes a credit reckoning, because the easiest way to grow a loan book is to lower the bar. The customers here are younger, often with limited credit history, which is the group most exposed to a weakening job market. Nothing in the numbers yet says the underwriting has slipped; everything in financial history says this is where to look.

The genuinely clever part of the model is the subscription. Instead of depending entirely on merchant fees per transaction, Sezzle charges consumers a monthly fee for access and flexibility — recurring revenue that arrives whether or not a purchase happens. That is roughly 40% of revenue and it is a structurally better income stream than transaction fees, because it is not cyclical with retail spending.

The structural defence of the model is duration: six-week plans mean credit problems surface within weeks rather than years, and the book can be tightened quickly as data arrives. That is a real advantage over conventional lenders. But at 28.1 times earnings and 8.5 times sales for a consumer lender growing this fast, with regulation tightening in several countries, the price assumes both the growth and the credit hold. Loss rates on the instalment book are the only number that settles it.
bull: Subscription revenue keeps growing as recurring income while six-week durations let the credit book be tightened fast, and underwriting holds through a soft consumer.
bear: Credit losses rise among young, thin-file borrowers, regulation imposes affordability checks and costs, and a 28 times earnings multiple on a lender collapses.
